Please review the following manuscript. I've poured months of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-rgj4be9m/call-6f26f9f4a73b473383c81056a36c6db0/manuscript.pdf

import importlib.util
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','pymupdf','PIL','pypdfium2']:

    print(name, s.origin if s else None)

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs
python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:', r.metadata)
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    t=p.extract_text()
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()[:27000])
PY"

for name, values in rows.items():

print('Table V non-linear loss relative decrease:',100*(.048-.039)/.048)

strengths: The research question has an identifiable audience in binary analysis and representation learning. Aligning source code, LLVM IR, and generated summaries offers a plausible way to transfer information into representations usable when source code is unavailable.

The BinaryCorp experiment provides the strongest empirical evidence: it evaluates x86-64 similarity across six optimization pairs and two candidate-pool sizes. For O0/O3 with pool size 1000, Table VII reports MRR increasing from GraphCodeBERT’s 0.108 to COMBO’s 0.129, with COMBO evaluated without downstream fine-tuning.

The architecture diagrams communicate the intended alignment and interpolation stages reasonably well. Public datasets, dataset statistics, and results broken down by optimization pair and vulnerability category provide a useful foundation for further investigation.
weaknesses: Necessary—Align the central claims with the evaluated representations. Pretraining and POJ-104 use compiler-generated LLVM IR, while Section V-D explicitly evaluates vulnerability analysis on source code. The manuscript therefore does not demonstrate the claimed three downstream tasks operating on binaries, particularly vulnerability detection in executable binaries. Either provide the corresponding evidence or consistently narrow the abstract, research questions, and conclusions. The existing x86 similarity experiment remains relevant under a narrower scope.

Necessary—Resolve substantial ambiguities in the evaluation protocols. Table II partitions POJ-104 into disjoint problem labels, yet Section V-B describes classification into 104 classes and evaluation across all classes without explaining how unseen labels are handled. Specify whether this is classification or retrieval and define its metrics and held-out evaluation. Section IV-B also ambiguously states that BinaryCorp training and test sets are used for fine-tuning. For vulnerability analysis, specify the split and reconcile Table IV’s normal examples with the description of classifying already-vulnerable snippets. These omissions prevent reliable interpretation of the reported results.

Necessary—Support the claimed benefits of individual components. Table V compares minimum validation losses from sequential stages with different representation pairs, learned targets, and training durations. Their decrease does not isolate interpolation’s contribution or establish improved downstream representations. Comparisons with matched training budgets, including ordinary contrastive training and removal of generated comments/interpolation stages, are needed for the component-superiority claims. The human gradual-learning explanation should remain a hypothesis unless independently supported.

Necessary—Make the implemented method sufficiently precise to reproduce. Equation (4) omits the softmax described in the prose, leaving Equation (5)’s cross-entropy targets unclear. Specify normalization, temperature, gradient handling through targets, and the exact intermediate objective. Encoder architectures and initialization, tokenization and truncation, pretraining settings, and the adaptation of GraphCodeBERT to LLVM/x86 inputs also need substantially more detail; referring generally to SimpleCLIP settings does not resolve these choices.

Necessary—Calibrate the comparative conclusions. The experiments compare against three language/source-code models but omit binary-specific methods such as the cited jTrans. Broad superiority claims require relevant comparisons, or should be restricted to the evaluated baselines. Several aggregate differences are small, including POJ-104 F1 of 0.700 versus 0.696 and vulnerability MacroF1 of 0.673 versus 0.671. Report uncertainty appropriate to claims of reliable improvement, or explicitly limit conclusions to the observed single-seed results. Acceptance does not require state-of-the-art performance.

Necessary—Reconcile numerical reporting and metric definitions. The headline 5.45% improvement lacks a specified baseline and aggregation rule. In Table VIII, COMBO’s six category F1 values average to 0.6665, matching the reported MicroF1 rather than MacroF1 of 0.673; explain the aggregation. Section V-D claims an arithmetic-category improvement although COMBO scores 0.640 versus GraphCodeBERT’s 0.651. Table V’s reduction from 0.048 to 0.039 is 18.75%, not 25.6%. Together with the protocol issues, these discrepancies leave the current manuscript short of the evidence and clarity required for acceptance.

Optional—Inspect generated-summary quality and learned interpolation weights to explain when the approach helps. Additional compiler and architecture settings would characterize transfer limits, but are not prerequisites for a carefully scoped contribution.
